name: Determining When to Buy a New Phone (Case 1)
description: Construct a program that determines whether it is time to buy a new phone based on the inputs that it receives from the user. A new phone should be bought if the phone breaks or the phone is at least 3 years old.
code:
#Step 1: Read the user inputs
text = input("Enter the phone age in years:")
phone_age = int(text)
text = input("Enter 1 if the phone is broken, otherwise enter 0:")
input_num = int(text)
#Step 2: Determine whether the phone is broken
if input_num == 1 :
    is_broken = True
else:
    is_broken = False
#Step 3: Write the boolean expression to determine whether it is time to buy a new phone
need_phone = is_broken or phone_age >= 3
#Step 4: Print the result
if need_phone == True :
    print("Yes! It is time to buy a new phone.")
else:
    print("No! It is not yet the time to buy a new phone.")

2.content: text = input("Enter the phone age in years:")
commentList: Purpose: This line asks the user for the phone age and saves what they type into the variable text so you can use it later in the program.

Syntax and meaning: input("Enter the phone age in years:") displays the prompt in quotes and waits for the user to type something; the = operator stores the returned value (always a string) into the variable named text.
How it behaves when running: when this line runs the program pauses and the prompt appears; the user must type a response and press Enter before the program continues.

Common misconceptions and errors: input always returns a string, so if the user types a number it is still text — converting it to an int later (int(text)) will fail with a ValueError if the user types non-numeric characters or leaves it blank.

Best practices: make the prompt clear (consider adding a space after the colon), use a more descriptive variable name like age_str or raw_age, and validate or strip the input (e.g., text = text.strip()) or use a try/except loop when converting to int so you handle invalid entries gracefully.

Alternative for compact code: you could combine reading and conversion (phone_age = int(input(...))) but keeping them separate, as here, makes it easier for you to check or clean the raw input before converting.

4.content: text = input("Enter 1 if the phone is broken, otherwise enter 0:")

Syntax and semantics: input(...) is a built‑in function that displays the string inside the quotes as a prompt and returns whatever the user types as a string; the = operator assigns that returned string to the variable text. The colon in the prompt is just part of the message shown to the user.

Common mistakes and errors: many learners type words like "yes"/"no" or "true"/"false"; since the program later does int(text), any non-numeric response (or an empty response) will cause a ValueError when converted to int. Also entering numbers other than 0 or 1 will not match the intended logic.

Best practices: make the prompt clear and accept common answers (for example show "Enter 1 for broken, 0 for not broken"). Validate the input before converting (for example use text = text.strip() and check text in ('0','1') or use try/except around int(text)). Use a more descriptive variable name like broken_input to avoid confusion with the earlier phone-age text variable.

Behavior note: input() pauses the program until the user presses Enter. Remember that input() always returns a string — you must convert or validate that string later (which this program does on the next line with int(text)).
